Objectivity. Analysts have to be aware of their own assumptions and actively work to identify and reduce bias, rather than letting familiar positions go unquestioned.

Products have to keep a clear line between the underlying intelligence and the analyst’s own assumptions and interpretations. That is the difference between “intercepted communications show X” and “we assess this means Y.” When the line blurs, policymakers can mistake an inference for a confirmed fact.

The ODNI Analytic Ombuds is the primary safeguard against politicized intelligence. The role addresses concerns about lack of objectivity, bias, politicization, or other failures in how the analytic standards are applied, and provides a confidential channel for analysts who believe they are being pressured to alter conclusions for reasons that have nothing to do with the evidence.

Congress created the position in the 2004 reform act, which required the DNI to designate someone available to counsel analysts, conduct arbitration, offer recommendations, and investigate complaints about biased or politicized analysis.
